# Harnessing AI in academic writing: The complex interplay of AI literacy and self-directed learning among university L2 learners

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

## Jian Xu

_School of Business English, Sichuan International Studies University, No. 33, Zhuangzhi Road, Lieshimu, Shapingba District, Chongqing, 400031, China_

## ARTICLE INFO ABSTRACT

### _Keywords:_ With the advancement of AI in the field of second/foreign (L2) language writing, AI literacy has 

AI literacy garnered increasing attention. This study investigated how AI literacy influences self-directed Self-directed learning learning (SDL) in the context of academic English writing among Chinese university students Academic English writing

and how they perceived AI literacy, SDL, and their relationships. Questionnaire and interview 

Mixed-method approach

data were collected and analyzed using structural equation modeling as well as open and axial coding. The quantitative results showed that the awareness of AI and ethical considerations positively predicted SDL, while the AI usage negatively predicted SDL, and evaluation had no significant relationship with SDL. The qualitative findings revealed that students found AI tools beneficial for completing academic writing tasks such as summarization and translation, emphasizing time efficiency and improved coherence. Additionally, they acknowledged AI’s effectiveness in providing timely written feedback and improving textual transitions. However, concerns were raised about the subject-specific reliability of AI, potential academic misconduct, and the impact on creativity, highlighting both the positive and negative impacts of AI literacy on SDL. Overall, the qualitative findings largely corroborated the quantitative results. The peda-

gogical implications are then discussed.

## 1. Introduction

As students engage more with artificial intelligence (AI), researchers advocate teaching them to evaluate the accuracy of AI- generated information, ([Pedro et al., 2019)](#appendix-a-supplementary-data), to explore the underlying mechanism of AI ([Miao & Shiohira, 2022)](#appendix-a-supplementary-data), and to discuss the ethical implications of AI ([Miao et al., 2021)](#appendix-a-supplementary-data), thereby being AI literate for the social good in general. AI refers to the ability of digital systems to complete tasks that are traditionally carried out by intelligent human beings. It trains computers to learn human behaviors, such as learning, evaluation, and decision-making (Xu et al., 2021). Situated in the second or foreign (L2) writing context, there is call for L2 learners to write in academic English with certain level of AI literacy as the effective use of AI tools can facilitate L2 learners’ writing process through translating their first language (L1) voice into English ([Sasaki, 2023)](#appendix-a-supplementary-data). Based on the findings of previous study on the definition of AI literacy in educational contexts (Wang et al., 2023), AI literacy in L2 academic writing is defined as a set of competencies related to the use of generative AI (GAI) technologies. These competencies include practical understanding of AI for academic writing purposes (awareness); proficiency in applying AI to complete academic writing tasks (usage); the ability to analyze, select, and critically evaluate AI-generated content (evaluation); and ethical awareness and moral implications associated with its use (ethics) in academic English writing contexts. AI literacy is not merely about the understanding of technology itself, but also about

Self-directed learning (SDL) is defined as “an approach where learners are motivated to assume personal responsibility and collaborative control of cognitive (self-monitoring) and contextual (self-management) processes in constructing and confirming meaningful and worthwhile learning outcomes” ([Garrison, 1997,](#appendix-a-supplementary-data) p. 18). The theory of planned behavior (TPB) provides a solid framework for understanding SDL in AI-assisted contexts. TPB posits that human behavior is driven by beliefs, subjective norms, and perceived behavioral control ([Ajzen, 2011)](#appendix-a-supplementary-data). SDL, as a behavioral outcome, can be influenced by the key constructs of the TPB. Ac- cording to the TPB, individuals tend to be more engaged, if their behaviors are expected to generate positive outcomes, if they perceive the behavior as socially acceptable, and if they believe they have control over performing the behavior ([Ajzen, 2011)](#appendix-a-supplementary-data). It has been justified that AI literacy can be incorporated into the TPB framework to account for human behavioral intention (Wang et al., 2025). In terms of using GAI to assist in L2 writers’ SDL, existing studies have been qualitatively conducted to explore YouTube content creators’ language learning experiences and the role of ChatGPT in their SDL ([Li, Bonk, et al., 2024)](#appendix-a-supplementary-data). How individuals self-direct their online language learning by using ChatGPT was also investigated ([Li, Wang, & Bonk, 2024)](#appendix-a-supplementary-data). Nevertheless, AI-assisted SDL is still a novel research area that deserves more research attention. Existing studies on GAI and academic writing primarily address the significance of empowering L2 learners with GAI literacy by implementing pedagogical interventions in L2 writing classrooms ([Nguyen et al., 2024;](#appendix-a-supplementary-data) [Pecorari, 2023)](#appendix-a-supplementary-data), introduce critical GAI literacy in doctoral academic writing ([Ou et al., 2024)](#appendix-a-supplementary-data), and examine the views and attitudes of L2 writing instructors regarding the integration of GAI in the L2 writing classrooms (Xu & Tan, 2024, 2025). Nevertheless, few studies have been conducted to explore the impacts of GAI literacy on learning behavior, especially SDL, among university students in the L2 writing context.

Against this backdrop, the current study attempts to address the existing knowledge gap by examining how the AI literacy of L2 writers influences their SDL in L2 writing contexts. The conceptualization of AI literacy in this study encompasses a broader inter- disciplinary understanding and is more characterized by its biological and social attributes ([Poria et al., 2017)](#appendix-a-supplementary-data). Examining the rela- tionship between AI literacy and SDL will allow instructors to implement targeted pedagogical interventions for effective integration of GAI tools, fostering L2 learners’ responsible and critical use, and helping them develop the critical awareness and proper skills needed to navigate the evolving landscape of academic English writing in the age of AI.

## 2. Literature review

### _2.1._ _AI literacy: theory and empirical research_

The term “literacy” initially refers to the skills and knowledge required for engaging with books and other printed materials ([McMillan, 1996)](#appendix-a-supplementary-data). AI literacy contains the specific competencies required to interact with and understand AI systems. Nowadays, AI has emerged as an innovative and transformative field of technology, capable of simulating, augmenting, and extending human in- telligence. This development has highlighted the importance of possessing AI literacy, a concept for demonstrating proficiency in utilizing advanced technologies to assist in academic English writing.

Wang et al. (2023) conceptualized AI literacy in the field of general education into four key components: awareness, usage, evaluation, and ethics. Awareness refers to a functional understanding of AI, and usage indicates the capability to effectively utilize AI in performing tasks. Evaluation means the ability to assess, choose, and critically reflect on AI-generated output and ethics refers to the understanding of ethical issues and moral considerations associated with its applications. While a number of previous studies have intensively examined human-AI collaboration in the academic writing contexts (e.g., [Bai & Nordin, 2025)](#appendix-a-supplementary-data), they have mainly focused on the functional roles of AI tools in shaping writing behavior and outcomes. In contrast, the present study shifts the focus toward L2 learners’ perceived AI literacy, including their awareness, usage, evaluation, and ethical considerations, and investigates how this perceived AI literacy influences SDL behaviors.

In spite of the growing recognition of AI literacy in the field of education, the number of empirical studies on this topic is increasing, especially in the field of L2 writing for academic purposes. Existing studies mainly focus on the conceptualization of AI literacy in the L2 writing contexts. For instance, Yi (2021) advocated AI literacy by highlighting the importance of understanding and evaluating AI-generated content or using AI tools effectively in writing, and emphasized that metacognition was a crucial component of AI literacy in evaluating sources and arguments. Unfortunately, the conceptualization of AI literacy in Yi’s (2021) study is not situated in the L2 context where academic English writing is taught to university students. To further conceptualize AI literacy in academic writing, [Ou et al. (2024)](#appendix-a-supplementary-data) conceptualized Critical GAI literacy and explored how critical a GAI literacy micro-curriculum can enhance PhD students’ abilities to self-regulate their AI tools-assisted writing for academic writing purposes. The findings showed that Critical GAI literacy comprises four dimensions, focusing on critical competencies in (1) interacting with AI, (2) understanding AI ethics in academic writing, (3) evaluating AI’s technical values and limitations, and (4) engaging in self-regulated learning. These dimensions formulated a theoretical framework for Critical GAI literacy, involving the knowledge and skills essential for doctoral students to write academically (see [Ou et al., 2024)](#appendix-a-supplementary-data). The conceptualization of [Ou et al.’s (2024)](#appendix-a-supplementary-data) study takes an initiative in including self-regulated writing behavior into the whole framework. In addition, Wang and Wang (2025) qualitatively investigated how L2 learners at ter- tiary level in the U.S. used ChatGPT to support their writing. Using a qualitative case study approach, they found that students utilized AI in different ways and identified four dimensions of critical AI literacy in writing: awareness, positionality, strategies, and evaluation.

Beyond conceptualizing AI literacy, recent studies have explored learners’ perceptions of and experiences with AI tools, showing a concern with enhancing learner agency and engagement. Instead of treating AI as a helper, studies consistently highlighted the importance of putting learners as agentive agents while navigating human-AI collaboration. Both [Jiang et al. (2024)](#appendix-a-supplementary-data) and [Ng et al. ](#appendix-a-supplementary-data)

[(2022)](#appendix-a-supplementary-data) valued the importance of cultivating learner agency in AI-supported writing and also highlighted the balanced and creative use of AI in learning settings. [Jiang et al. (2024)](#appendix-a-supplementary-data) examined undergraduate students’ perceptions of agency and authorship in AI-assisted academic writing. Through narrative analysis of students’ interactions with ChatGPT, they found that students adopt a balanced stance in their use of ChatGPT during the writing process, and they also recognized both human and AI contributions without over-attributing agency to technologies. Similarly, [Ng et al. (2022)](#appendix-a-supplementary-data) showed that digital story writing was an effective inquiry-based approach to cultivate AI literacy among primary school students by enabling them to apply AI knowledge to real-life and problem-solving settings. The above studies indicated that effective AI literacy instruction should go beyond simple technical proficiency to create opportunities for language learners to critically evaluate and integrate AI tools into their own creative language learning practices. The present study adopts the definitions of AI literacy proposed by Wang et al. (2023) in the field of general education. Different from [Ou et al.’s (2024)](#appendix-a-supplementary-data) focus on Critical GAI literacy within a PhD-level micro-curriculum, which emphasized more advanced critical engagement, Wang et al.’s (2023) framework is broader and more adaptable for studying L2 writers. Additionally, Wang et al.’s (2023) framework integrates both technical and ethical dimensions necessary for effective and self-directed use of AI tools, making it well-suited for investigating how these competencies foster SDL behaviors in academic writing environments. Awareness helps L2 learners understand how AI can assist with academic writing tasks like drafting and editing. Usage enables them to use AI tools effectively to improve writing quality. Evaluation allows L2 learners to assess and refine AI-generated content to meet academic writing standards. Ethics ensures responsible use, promotes academic integrity, and reduces plagiarism in writing practices. Each component of Wang et al.’s (2023) framework is considered distinct and significant for examining L2 writers’ abilities of under- standing, integrating, and evaluating AI tools into academic English writing.

### _2.2._ _AI literacy as an antecedent of learning behavior_

AI literacy can be considered a key factor that shapes and influences subsequent learning behaviors. [Chai et al. (2021)](#appendix-a-supplementary-data) quantita- tively examined the relationship between AI literacy and other variables in the primary school contexts. They found that AI literacy influenced students’ self-efficacy, which in turn significantly predicted behavioral intention, but AI literacy did not influence behavioral intention directly. Wang et al. (2025) examined the factors influencing Chinese university students’ intentions to use AI technology. Using structural equation modeling and interviews methods, they found that students’ attitudes toward AI significantly predicted their intention to use it; AI literacy in ethics was scored highest, while AI awareness was lowest among literacy components. Both AI literacy and subjective norms positively influenced university students’ attitudes and perceived behavioral control. Interviews further highlighted implications for creating AI-integrated educational ecosystems in universities. Despite the exploration of the in- fluences of AI literacy on self-efficacy and behavioral intention, existing studies still fail to examine whether the level of AI literacy possessed by L2 writers influences their actual learning behaviors, such as the use of self-directed writing strategies. Examining SDL in the context of academic English writing is crucial for developing autonomous, reflective, and adaptable L2 writers.

### _2.3._ _Self-directed learning: theory and empirical studies_

The concept of SDL has been extensively researched for decades (e.g., [Brockett & Hiemstra, 2018;](#appendix-a-supplementary-data) [Gibbons, 2002)](#appendix-a-supplementary-data). [Brookfield (2013)](#appendix-a-supplementary-data) emphasized the significance of making decisions for learners in terms of what to learn, when to learn, and the degree of learning, reflecting whether they have mastered the learning material sufficiently. Likewise,[ Sze-Yeng and Hussain (2010)](#appendix-a-supplementary-data) [u](#appendix-a-supplementary-data)nderscored the importance of researching learner autonomy from the perspective of personal attributes. Based on this perspective, [Tekkol and Demirel (2018)](#appendix-a-supplementary-data) further elaborated on SDL by defining self-directed learners as individuals who were able to learn independently, control their own learning processes, transfer newly acquired knowledge to broader contexts, and effectively address academic challenges. After reviewing the literature, we found that [Garrison’s (1997)](#appendix-a-supplementary-data) SDL framework is a widely acknowledged model and it conceptualizes SDL into three key components: self-management, self-monitoring, and motivation.

Compared with [Knowles’ (1975)](#appendix-a-supplementary-data) process-oriented SDL model, which primarily focuses on goal-setting and resource identification, [Garrison’s (1997)](#appendix-a-supplementary-data) framework emphasizes the dynamic interaction between cognitive, metacognitive, and motivational processes, which is more applicable to technology-enhanced learning environments. Self-management refers to the learner’s ability to plan, organize, and manage their time, resources, and learning behaviors in specific conditions. Self-monitoring refers to learners’ abilities to be engaged in metacognition, including the processes of reflecting on and controlling their cognitive and metacognitive thinking. The present study selected self-monitoring and self-management to indicate SDL behaviors as both constructs represent essential behav- ioral dimensions of how learners self-direct their behavior during the learning process. However, motivation primarily represents a psychological state rather than observable behaviors. The present study investigate the impact of AI literacy, including awareness, usage, evaluation, and ethics (Wang et al., 2023), on self-directed behaviors. Since self-monitoring and self-management are more appropriate as the behavior-oriented measures in academic English writing contexts, self-management and self-monitoring will be treated as two independent variables in the present study.

Empirical investigations of SDL in English writing contexts remain limited, with only two notable studies directly addressing SDL in the writing process. Specifically, [Choy and Cheung (2022)](#appendix-a-supplementary-data) showcased that Singaporean primary school students had a positive attitude towards SDL; information and communication technologies-supported activities can effectively foster SDL and collaborative learning skills, especially in blended or online writing contexts. [Chen and Tsou (2024)](#appendix-a-supplementary-data) explored how translingual practices can help Taiwanese first-year college English majors in developing SDL skills for English writing. Findings revealed that translingual awareness enhanced students’ translingual awareness, thereby improving their SDL and enhancing English writing proficiency. However, more empirical studies are still needed to examine SDL in the context of academic English.

### _2.4._ _Theoretical foundation and empirical studies regarding the role of AI in SDL_

According to social cognitive theory ([Bandura, 1986)](#appendix-a-supplementary-data), there exists a dynamic interaction among individual factors, environmental influences, and human behavior. An individual’s learning occurs through interactions with the social environment. Specifically, in- dividuals develop skills and acquire knowledge through interaction with their environment, such as digital tools, and interaction with their individual beliefs, such as the confidence in one’s capabilities to succeed in specific tasks when engaged in the learning process. AI literacy, including awareness, usage, evaluation, and ethics (Wang et al., 2023) in English academic writing can be viewed as a epistemic factor which is related to knowledge and understanding, and the behavioral aspects of SDL (i.e., self-management and self-monitoring) can be considered part of human behaviors. AI literacy may empower L2 learners with the knowledge and skills to effectively use AI tools for academic writing purposes and thus elicit learners’ greater autonomy in managing their writing tasks. For example, ChatGPT provides instant feedback on grammar, coherence, and vocabulary use with L2 learners. L2 learners who know how to use these tools critically can monitor their writing progress and refine their writing drafts, thereby improving their abilities of self-regulating the writing process without merely relying on teachers. Thus, in the digital learning environment, AI literacy in aca- demic writing may play a significant role in facilitating SDL.

Behavioral intention is influenced by various factors that include individual (e.g., personality), societal (e.g., age and gender), and epistemic (e.g., knowledge and thinking patterns) categories ([Fishbein & Ajzen, 2011)](#appendix-a-supplementary-data). AI literacy in academic writing can be grounded in epistemic categories. According to the theory of planned behavior ([Fishbein & Ajzen, 2011)](#appendix-a-supplementary-data), AI literacy forms the foundation of behavioral, normative, and control beliefs, which in turn influences behavioral intention. Specifically, individuals with a higher level of AI literacy are more likely to hold positive behavioral beliefs about AI use, be aware of normative expectations from peers or institutions with regard to appropriate AI use, and have stronger control beliefs about their abilities to use AI tools effectively. These informed beliefs together contribute to the formation of a strong behavioral intention to engage with AI technologies. These explanations offer insight into the relationship between AI literacy and SDL (i.e., self-management and self-monitoring) in the context of academic English writing among university L2 learners.

A robust theoretical lens for explaining the connections between AI literacy and SDL in the context of academic English writing is self-regulated learning (SRL) theory, particularly as articulated by Zimmerman and Schunk (2011). The SRL theory features meta- cognitive processes in which planning, monitoring, and evaluation are involved. These processes are significant to autonomous and reflective learning. In AI-assisted writing contexts, AI literacy functions as a critical facilitator of SRL. L2 learners who are AI literate will be more likely to engage at different SRL phases: they can plan how to use AI tools, monitor AI-generated outcomes through checking relevance and accuracy, and assess the quality of their own writing. SDL and SRL are related and similar, but the scope of SDL is larger, which contains formal and informal learning.

The digital revolution has positioned SDL at the forefront. The first line of research had growing interest in how digitally mediated environments and learning tools shape the SDL. Research has consistently shown that technological tools themselves or group and collaborative learning in digital environments enhanced student engagement and fostered the development of SDL, both of which are critical for academic success ([Aflalo et al., 2024;](#appendix-a-supplementary-data) [Rashid & Asghar, 2016)](#appendix-a-supplementary-data). To effectively foster SDL, it is important to develop not only technological competencies but also a pedagogical understanding of engaging learners in selecting and using digital tools that align with their educational needs ([Aflalo et al., 2024)](#appendix-a-supplementary-data). The second line of studies focused on the application of AI in SDL in formal English writing, although the number of empirical studies remains limited. Evidence suggests that students are likely to have a strong sense of responsibility and employ a range of self-management strategies when interacting with AI tools to write, although the use of self-monitoring remains limited; nonetheless, critical reflection to verify AI-generated content appears to be common, pointing to growing metacognitive engagement of postsecondary writers ([Wang et al., 2024)](#appendix-a-supplementary-data). Findings of a longitudinal study further indicated a reciprocal relationship between SDL and critical thinking over time. While the connection between critical thinking skills, SDL competency, and AI-assisted writing proficiency was more unidirectional, SDL has been evidenced to moderate the influence of critical thinking on writing performance during two time points but not during the third, suggesting a dynamic role for SDL in influencing academic writing outcomes ([Shen & Teng, 2024)](#appendix-a-supplementary-data). These findings highlight the complex and developed nature of SDL in AI-assisted writing environments. The third line of research addressed key stakeholders’ perceptions of ChatGPT in facilitating SDL. [Li, Bonk, et al. (2024)](#appendix-a-supplementary-data) explored the role of ChatGPT in self-directed language learning among YouTube content creators, and they proposed a refined SDL framework that addresses both personal learning dynamics and the broader socio-cultural impact of AI. They also examined YouTube language educators’ perceptions of ChatGPT in self-directed language learning, and they found the value of ChatGPT for improving learning through accessibility, versatility, and contextual support ([Li, Wang, et al., 2024)](#appendix-a-supplementary-data). A study involving language learners also emphasized ChatGPT’s value in encouraging language learners to use AI because of its adaptability and personalized features, and highlighted learners’ self-monitoring skills that supported more effective use of ChatGPT, eventually enabling the attainment of their learning goals ([Li, Wang, & Bonk, 2024)](#appendix-a-supplementary-data).

The above reviewed studies primarily focus on specific groups, such as postsecondary writers in the U.S. ([Wang et al., 2024)](#appendix-a-supplementary-data) or YouTube content creators ([Li, Wang, et al., 2024)](#appendix-a-supplementary-data). While these studies emphasize the vital role of SDL in AI-assisted writing contexts and examine the impact of SDL on students’ writing processes, they did not address how the behavioral aspects of SDL—self-ma- nagement and self-monitoring—are influenced by AI literacy from university L2 writers’ perspectives. Besides, existing studies have seldom used a mixed-methods approach to examine university L2 learners’ AI literacy and SDL in the contexts of academic English writing (see the predominance of non-mixed designs: [Li, Bonk, et al., 2024;](#appendix-a-supplementary-data) Wang & Wang, 2025). To address these gaps, this study is guided by the following research questions: 

***RQ1***: What are the relationships between AI literacy and SDL as reported by university L2 learners through questionnaires in the context of academic English writing?

***RQ2***: How do L2 learners perceive the use of AI tools and their SDL based on their interview responses in the context of academic English writing?

## 3. Method

A concurrent embedded mixed-method design ([Creswell & Plano-Clark, 2017)](#appendix-a-supplementary-data) was employed to address the two research questions. The design started with the collection and analysis of quantitative data to investigate the relationship between AI literacy and SDL in the context of academic English writing (research question 1). This was followed by a qualitative inquiry intended to capture how L2 learners perceived their AI literacy, SDL, and the relationships between AI literacy and SDL (research question 2). Such a mixed-method approach can enable the triangulation of quantitative results and qualitative findings ([Creswell & Plano-Clark, 2017)](#appendix-a-supplementary-data), offering a deeper understanding of the interplay between AI literacy and SDL by showcasing details that quantitative data alone could not reveal.

### _3.1._ _Context and participants_

This study was conducted in the context of Chinese universities, where English is an L2 for students and they learned academic English writing in their second or third year of undergraduate studies. In the English academic writing course, students were required to focus on the academic writing process and develop sufficient skills to write structured and coherent academic texts in English. Planning, drafting, editing, and revision were practiced, and sentence-level grammar is an important area of concern, with particular attention paid to its accurate use and structure. The course is designed to help students grasp the knowledge and skills that are necessary to write academically in an appropriate way after conducting academic research.

A valid sample of 309 participants completed the questionnaires after removing cases with missing data and duplicated responses. The age of participants ranged from 18 to 24 years (_M_ = 20.74, _SD_ = .86). There were 43 male students (13.9 %) and 266 female students (86.1 %). Participants were all English majors. Most participants had upper-intermediate English proficiency, having suc- cessfully passed the College English Test Band 4 (CET-4), a large-scale and high-stakes English proficiency test in China. The par- ticipants’ first language was Chinese, and they were learning English to prepare for future job opportunities or applications for master’s programs.

A maximum variation sampling strategy was employed to identify and select potential interviewees. It is a purposive sampling strategy used in qualitative research to select participants to capture a broad range of their experiences that arise from adapting to different circumstances ([Patton, 2002)](#appendix-a-supplementary-data). A total of six participants, who had previously indicated their willingness to participate in follow-up interviews via the questionnaire, were invited and interviewed. [Table 1](#3-method) provides a summary of the interviewees’ key de- mographic information (pseudonyms used to protect identities). The six interviewees were selected to represent varying levels of AI literacy and SDL, with three demonstrating high levels and three low levels based on mean score. This variation allows for the exploration of patterns across different learners, enhancing the depth of the qualitative data ([Patton, 2002)](#appendix-a-supplementary-data). All interviewees had Chinese as their first language. They have upper to intermediate English proficiency, as all of them have passed the College English Test Band 4 (CET-4). They were second-year undergraduate students with experience in practicing academic English writing both inside and outside the classroom, and they frequently used AI tools to support their writing. Among the interviewees, there were five female students and one male student.

### _3.2._ _Measures_

#### _3.2.1._ _Scale of AI literacy in academic writing_

The present study adapted Wang et al.’s (2023) AI literacy scale to fit into the context of academic English writing. The 12-item scale includes four dimensions: awareness (3 items), usage (3 items), evaluation (3 items), and ethics (3 items). This scale was selected because it has a comprehensive coverage of key competencies involved in AI literacy, which are relevant to effective and ethical use of AI tools in academic writing. The original 12-item scale was carefully reviewed by the researcher to ensure its content relevance and appropriateness for L2 learners. Each item of the original scale was modified slightly by incorporating the phrase “academic English writing” to ensure domain specificity. Awareness means the abilities to identify and understand AI technology when

using AI-driven applications to write academic English (e.g., “I know how AI technology can help me to write academically in En- glish”). Usage denotes the abilities to effectively make use of AI technology to complete academic English writing tasks (e.g., “I can use AI applications or products to improve my academic English writing efficiency”). Evaluation refers to the abilities to analyze, choose, and critically assess AI applications and their outcomes when employed for academic English writing (e.g., “I can choose the most appropriate AI application or product from a variety for an academic English writing task”). Ethics refers to the abilities to understand the responsibilities and potential risks when using AI technology for academic English writing (e.g., “I am always alert to the abuse of AI technology in academic English writing”). To ensure cultural and linguistic appropriateness, two experts in L2 writing had been invited to review the adapted items, and a pilot test was conducted with two L2 learners, leading to further improvements based on their constructive feedback. Participants rated the questionnaires on a 5-point Likert scale from 1 = ‘strongly disagree’ to 5 = ‘strongly agree’. The reliability of the scale was high, indicated by an overall Cronbach’s α of .87. The reliability of awareness, usage, evaluation, and ethics was acceptable as the Cronbach’s α was .73, .78, .75, and .75, respectively.

#### _3.2.2._ _Scale of SDL_

The present study used [Wang et al.’s (2024)](#appendix-a-supplementary-data) SDL scale to measure university students’ behavioral aspects of SDL in the context of academic English writing. This scale was chosen because it focuses on the behavioral aspects of SDL, which are central to this study’s aim of investigating how university students manage and monitor their learning process in academic English writing. The 14-item scale includes two dimensions: self-management (11 items) and self-monitoring (3 items). Each item of the original scale was modified slightly by incorporating the phrase “academic English writing” to ensure domain specificity. The sample item for self-management was “I am organized while learning academic English writing with AI”. The sample item for self-monitoring was “I critically eval- uate new ideas related to academic writing learning provided by AI”. Participants rated the questionnaires on a 5-point Likert scale from 1 = ‘strongly disagree’ to 5 = ‘strongly agree’. The reliability of the overall scale was high, indicated by a Cronbach’s α of .89. The reliability of self-management and self-monitoring was good, too, as the Cronbach’s α was .86 and .80, respectively. The questionnaire items for both scales are provided in Appendix I.

### _3.3._ _Data collection_

Questionnaire data were collected in the Fall academic semester of 2024. The convenience sampling strategy was employed to recruit potential participants. The following criteria were followed to select survey participants: first, Year 2 and Year 3 students were targeted, because they had been exposed to academic English writing for over one year or more; second, participants had completed the academic English writing course and thus had experiences of utilizing AI tools in their academic writing practices. The first author contacted the faculty staff in two homogeneous universities where an academic English writing course was taught to undergraduate students. The two selected research-based universities were key universities at the provincial level located in the urban areas in the Southwestern part of China, and they were established five decades ago with relatively large number ofstaff and students. The faculty staff subsequently approached colleagues from the same faculty to assist in distributing the questionnaires during a 10-min class interval. An electronic version of the questionnaires was thus distributed to participants via the _Wenjuanxing_ platform by the faculty staff. Participants scanned the QR code and then filled in the questionnaires.It took participants approximately 5 minutes to complete the questionnaire. Prior to data collection, participants were informed about the research purposes and assured of the confidentiality of their responses. Informed consent was obtained from participants, after which data collection proceeded. A small monetary incentive was offered to compensate them for their participation. After removing missing data, duplicate, and blank responses, a sample of 309 participants was finally obtained. Missing data were addressed by using listwise deletion, because this approach can minimize biased statistics generated from a variance–covariance matrix, such as the regression coefficients ([Cox et al., 2014)](#appendix-a-supplementary-data). To gain deeper insights into participants’ academic writing experiences, semi-structured interviews were conducted while the questionnaire survey was distributed to participants. Informed consent was obtained from all interviewees, and the interview data were pseudonymized to ensure confidentiality. During the interviews, participants elaborated on their experiences and perceptions of using AI technology in academic English writing, as well as the self-directed activities they had done while writing English for aca- demic purposes. All interviews, which lasted approximately 30 min, were conducted individually in the participants’ mother tongue (Mandarin Chinese) to facilitate clear, accurate, and comfortable communication. The audio-recorded interviews were then tran- scribed verbatim for subsequent qualitative analysis.

### _3.4._ _Data analysis_

To address Research Question 1, structural equation modeling (SEM) was employed to investigate the relationships between AI literacy and SDL in the context of academic English writing. SEM allows for analyzing complex relationships among multiple inde- pendent and multiple dependent variables simultaneously. SEM can also accommodate latent variables, address measurement error, and provide robust model fit assessment, making it an effective tool for testing hypothesized theoretical models ([Kline, 2023)](#appendix-a-supplementary-data). The calculation was performed in Amos 26 with maximum likelihood estimation. Initially, confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) was con- ducted to test two distinct measurement models: one for AI literacy in academic English writing and the other for SDL for academic English writing. Model evaluation was conducted by referring to multiple fit indices, including the Comparative Fit Index (CFI), Tucker-Lewis Index (TLI), the Root Mean Square Error of Approximation (RMSEA), and the Standardized Root Mean Residual (SRMR). Based on [Kline’s (2023)](#appendix-a-supplementary-data) criteria, acceptable model fit was determined when CFI and TLI were greater than .90, with RMSEA and SRMR being below .08. The hypothesized SEM model was formed based on relevant theories and existing empirical studies, which is 

displayed in [Fig. 1.](#4-quantitative-results) To address Research Question 2, thematic analysis was conducted for the qualitative interview data, with codes, categories, and themes inductively derived ([Strauss & Corbin, 1998)](#appendix-a-supplementary-data). The process of thematic analysis started with repeated readings of the Chinese transcripts to identify frequent and recurring words, phrases, and sentences in relation to AI literacy and SDL. Through open coding, initial codes were generated that captured distinct elements of their writing experiences, such as how they used AI for planning, revised based on AI-generated feedback, or reflected on ethical concerns. These codes were then systematically organized and grouped into meaningful categories, such as AI-supported self-management and self-monitoring practices. Axial coding was followed, allowing for the comparison and integration of the same or overlapping codes and categories, concentrating on interviewees’ illustrations of AI literacy and SDL in relation to academic English writing. Themes were finally generated which identified common themes across interviewees. Although the qualitative sample consisted of six participants, data saturation was considered to be reached when there were no new codes emerged in the final two interviews, indicating thematic redundancy. The researcher and the research assistant coded part of the data independently and reached an agreement of 89%. Discrepancies were addressed through mutual discussion between two experienced researchers in the present study. Last, member checking was conducted to ensure the validity and reliability of the whole coding process ([Birt et al., 2016)](#appendix-a-supplementary-data).

## 4. Quantitative results

In this section, we first present the quantitative results to elucidate the relationships between AI literacy and SDL in the context of academic English writing. This is followed by an in-depth analysis of the qualitative interview data, which explores and identifies relevant themes in greater details to triangulate or provide deeper insights into the quantitative results in another section.

### _4.1._ _Descriptive and correlation analyses for latent variables_

Normality of the questionnaire data was assessed prior to data analysis. Both kurtosis and skewness values fell within the range of − 2 to +2, suggesting no violations of normal distribution. [Table 2](#43-structural-equation-models-to-examine-the-relationship-between-ai-literacy-and-sdl-rq1) presents the results of descriptive statistics, including mean and standard deviation, as well as _Pearson_ correlation coefficients between four independent variables (awareness, usage, evaluation, and ethics) and two dependent variables (self-management and self-monitoring). Overall, students reported high levels of AI literacy, as reflected in the fact that the mean scores of all four latent variables were above 3.5. Particularly, the mean score of ethics was above 4. This descriptive result suggests that students are AI literate when writing in English for academic purposes. Similarly, students demonstrated upper-middle levels of SDL activities, as the mean scores of both latent variables were greater than 3.5 and almost 4. This suggests that students are generally self-directed when using AI to write in English for academic purposes. The results of _Pearson_ correlation analyses demonstrated significant positive correlations among six latent variables. [Table 2](#43-structural-equation-models-to-examine-the-relationship-between-ai-literacy-and-sdl-rq1) details the bivariate _Pearson_ correlation coefficients between the latent variables, which ranged from .29 to .70. These results indicated significant relationships between AI literacy and SDL in the context of academic English writing. The correlation results served as initial findings, which laid a foundation for subsequent SEM analysis.

### _4.2._ _The measurement models for AI literacy and SDL_

Two measurement models were constructed. One is for AI literacy-related variables, and the other is for SDL-related variables. The measurement models were evaluated through the use of confirmatory factor analyses (CFA), with all latent variables being represented by their corresponding observed items. Regarding the four latent variables of AI literacy in academic writing, the measurement model

Regarding the two latent variables of SDL in academic English writing, the measurement model fit the empirical data adequately, too (χ[^2]/df = 2.97, _p \<_ .001, CFI = .92, RMSEA = .08, SRMR = .05).

### _4.3._ _Structural equation models to examine the relationship between AI literacy and SDL (RQ1)_

In the hypothesized SEM model (see [Fig. 2)](#43-structural-equation-models-to-examine-the-relationship-between-ai-literacy-and-sdl-rq1), the predictive roles of AI literacy in SDL had been revealed. This SEM model yielded a satisfactory model fit to the empirical data (χ[^2]/df = 2.27, _p \<_ .001, CFI = .90, RMSEA = .06, SRMR = .06). According to the stan- dardized coefficients as shown in [Fig. 2,](#43-structural-equation-models-to-examine-the-relationship-between-ai-literacy-and-sdl-rq1) awareness positively predicted self-management (_β_ = .53, _p \<_ .05) and self-monitoring (_β_ = .55, _p \<_ .05). Usage negatively predicted self-management (_β_ = − .25, _p \<_ .05) and self-monitoring (_β_ = − .31, _p \<_ .05). Ethics positively predicted self-management (_β_ = .38, _p \<_ .01) and self-monitoring (_β_ = .53, _p \<_ .01). Unfortunately, evaluation did not significantly predict self-management and self-monitoring. The SEM results indicated that a higher level of awareness and ethical considerations in AI technology in the context of academic English writing contributed to a greater use of self-management and self-monitoring stra- tegies. In contrast, the increasing usage of AI technology led to less frequent use of self-management and self-monitoring strategies. There was no relationship between the evaluation of AI-generated information and the use of self-management and monitoring strategies. A robustness check involving the use of the female-only sub-sample generated consistent model estimates, indicating that the structural relationships between AI literacy and SDL were consistent in the dominant sex group. However, because of the small size of the male sub-sample, multi-group SEM across gender was not feasible to be performed. In addition, to address potential confounding effects, academic year was included as a control variable together with age and gender in the SEM. The key structural paths between AI literacy and SDL remained statistically significant and consistent, meaning that the original structural relationships were robust to demographic variation (i.e., age, gender, & academic year).

## 5. Qualitative findings (_RQ2_)

### _5.1._ _AI acts as a functional tool in academic English writing_

Participants mentioned the utility of AI tools in academic English writing, particularly emphasizing their efficiency and support. This, to some extent, explains how AI tools can be effectively integrated into the academic writing process. For instance, Leah explained, 

**Fig. 2.** The structural relationships between AI literacy and SDL in academic English writing. _Note_: \*_p \<_ .05, \*\*_p \<_ .01; the observed variables and measurement errors were not drawn here for simplicity purposes.

_"I think it can be helpful because, at the beginning, when I first started using it, I felt that, for the most part, people (including myself) might initially have a mindset of wanting to take shortcuts when using AI. However, after using it, I realized that it can help us save a lot of time when I need to summarize or translate academic texts." (Leah)_

Leah acknowledged that AI tools offered a “shortcut” for academic writing tasks. However, she emphasized that the main benefit she gained is the substantial saving of time. The participant used AI tools primarily to receive practical support, such as summarization and translation, to enhance efficiency.

In addition, most participants viewed AI tools as an alternative to instructor-based assessment, providing timely and useful feedback for independent academic writing. For example, Maria illustrated: 

_First, I think it can evaluate our academic writing, like a teacher grading it and giving advice. We don’t need to trouble the teacher, and we can directly use it for evaluation purposes._

It seems that the most beneficial aspect of AI tools was the ability to evaluate their writing and offer constructive feedback, which functioned similarly to an instructor. AI allowed for self-assessment and enables students to make progress in academic writing, reducing the workload on human instructors while providing timely academic support to students. The above quote also presented a decreasing sense of learner agency in self-assessing their written work, but an increasing agency of using AI for feedback. In addition to its evaluation function, the participants perceived AI tools as effective in increasing academic writing quality. Fiona explained: 

_When I’m working on linking different sections of my academic writing, I often feel that the transitions aren’t very smooth. Using AI could potentially help restructure my writing more naturally and fluently._

The participant explicitly acknowledged difficulty in making smooth transitions between different sections of academic writing. AI tools can help in finetuning the transitions between paragraphs, contributing to the overall coherence of the structure. This suggested an expectation of AI assistance beyond grammar checks. This has been recognized as a key area where AI can be very useful in ac- ademic writing contexts.

In the process of using AI for academic English writing, participants also expressed their ethical concerns. They encountered challenges, particularly in terms of subject-specific reliability, academic misconduct, and creativity. 

_Different AI systems have their own areas of expertise … Especially when it comes to legal documents, those related to domestic law._ AI _might even provide incorrect answers_—_what may be correct in a foreign context could be completely inapplicable in the domestic context. (Yara)_

_Mentioning AI often causes a lot of alarm, as if using AI automatically means you’re engaging in academic misconduct or plagiarism. However, I believe it depends on the individual. AI is just a tool, and its appropriate use in academic writing is what matters_—_the key is still our responsibility.” (Kyle)_

_“AI’s creative thinking in academic writing cannot function like the human brain, which is able to consider multiple perspectives. For a given writing topic, AI may only come up with one particular example/perspective, which results in a situation where many people find out information on the same topic and end up with results limited to just a few options.” (Fiona)_

The above quotes first reflected limitations in the capabilities of AI tools—their overly reliance on data sources that may not completely align with local specialized knowledge and lack of the versatility or creativity of human thought, which may likely result in ethical concerns. The participant acknowledged the fear of academic misconduct when using AI, but also emphasized the importance of being aware of and responsible use of AI to avoid academic dishonesty. Students were aware of the negative consequences of that could arise if AI was improperly used. However, the ethical issues should go beyond the written product to consider how AI influences students’ writing beliefs, behaviors, and habits in an undesirable way calls for future attention.

### _5.2._ _The use of AI and SDL activities_

Two participants (Leah & Talia) reported the need to strike a balance between using AI tools for assistance in academic writing and maintaining a self-directed state in the process of writing, making sure that AI will not replace their initiative or agency. For instance, one participant articulated: 

_“Yes, because times are changing … You can’t entirely rely on yourself to learn in a traditional and hard way. (Leah)_

This insight seems to advocate for a pragmatic approach where AI can be viewed as an aid instead of a replacement. In terms of the relationship between AI tools and SDL in the context of academic English writing, participants expressed their understandings. For example, 

_“When I start working on an academic paper, I need to collect various materials myself and construct a writing framework, which is a time-consuming and labor-intensive process. However, AI makes academic writing a bit easier, which positively influences my moti-_ _vation. I think, to be honest, when there’s a very effective tool available, it’s likely that people’s initiative to do things entirely on their own won’t be so strong, and they might not feel inclined to rely merely on themselves from start to finish.” (Maria)_

It can be inferred that AI helped gather information and offered an initial writing framework in the planning stage, which reduced 

the overall workload. However, the participant also recognized the possibility of overuse of AI, which can prevent the development of self-directed writing skills. This recognition was associated with the “crutch effect” of AI, where overreliance may diminish the L2 learner’s ability to perform academic writing tasks agentively without assistance.

Additionally, participants clearly expressed the negative impacts of AI on the self-directed process in academic English writing. The increased convenience provided by AI tools led participants to rely heavily on AI for guidance and feedback, which diminished their engagement in their own self-directed processes. The following excerpts served as illustrative examples. 

_“Our thought processes might become simplified, as we may assign all the cognitive tasks that our brains should have performed to AI. This could probably lead us to become more reliant and prone to laziness.” (Fiona)_

_“As AI, a convenient and efficient tool, becomes available, we may lose some of our motivation to perform tasks independently.” (Leah)._

Instead of using critical thinking in problem-solving, participants relied on AI for suggestions, which reduced the need for self- monitoring to verify their writing progress actively. The availability of AI also diminished participants’ intrinsic motivation to engage in all writing stages. This reduced effort to deal with each aspect of the writing task—from planning and drafting to final revising—indicated a decreased use of self-management strategies. Both pointed to a cognitive threat: although AI provides solutions and efficiency, excessive use may undermine learners’ own agentive and independent thought, and consistent analytical engagement, both central to critical thinking in academic writing.

In contrast, AI, to some extent, fostered students’ SDL and writing motivation. This point can be supported by most participants. Among them, Yara illustrated: 

_“I believe AI can facilitate my SDL after class. In the classroom setting, I might only passively complete my academic writing tasks. Using AI has become a process of self-improvement for me after class. I need to evaluate whether the corrections it provides to me are accurate and make judgments about the given results.”_

It was suggested that AI can positively foster writing autonomy outside of the classroom. In other words, it empowered L2 learners to take control of their own writing process after class. The participant also perceived that while it provided support, L2 learners need to critically evaluate its feedback. Although the process of academic writing was complex, learners’ evaluation and reflection process triggered their SDL.

## 6. Discussion

### _6.1._ _Triangulation of quantitative results and qualitative findings_

Generally, the qualitative findings align with the quantitative results in several ways. Participants thought that AI tools can enhance their efficiency in academic writing by offering timely feedback and improving coherence, which, to some extent, corresponds to the quantitative SEM results that a higher level of awareness of AI positively predicted self-management and self-monitoring. This suggests that understanding AI’s capabilities facilitates L2 learners’ proactive learning strategies in the process of English academic writing. Additionally, participants highlighted the importance of ethical considerations when using AI for academic writing purposes. How- ever, concerns about over-reliance on AI with reduced self-reflection can potentially hinder SDL, which partially supports the quantitative results that increased AI usage negatively predicts SDL. This indicates a critical tension in AI-assisted academic English writing: although AI can actually support SDL, uncritical or excessive use may undermine the effectiveness of SDL. The results highlight the need for a balanced and mindful integration of AI tools in academic English writing contexts, where effective use of AI requires both strong awareness and ethical considerations to enhance SDL.

### _6.2._ _The positive impacts of awareness and ethics on SDL in academic English writing_

Partly consistent with what[ Aflalo et al.,(2024),](#appendix-a-supplementary-data) [Rashid and Asghar (2016),](#appendix-a-supplementary-data) and [Shen and Teng (2024)](#appendix-a-supplementary-data) have found, the present study showcases the positive impacts of awareness of AI technology on SDL. However, the present study is uniquely situated in the context of academic English writing. The findings indicate that L2 learners who understand AI technology may take more initiative in their English writing practices, engage in self-assessment and feedback-seeking, and seek writing improvement. However, the finding of this study is slightly different from [Chai et al.’s (2021)](#appendix-a-supplementary-data) findings that the construct of AI literacy did not predict primary school students’ behavioral intention to use AI. Our study shows that L2 learners’ ethical consideration when using AI in academic English writing will positively predict SDL. It means that the more ethical considerations L2 learners hold (e.g., subject-specific reliability, potential ac- ademic misconduct, and the impacts on creativity), the more SDL strategies they will use in their writing process. To explain this unique finding, the ethical awareness of L2 learners pushes them to take control of their writing process, seek out necessary resources, and employ effective strategies to produce written work that is accurate, original, and ethically sound. This not only helps them develop their academic English writing skills ([Wang et al., 2024)](#appendix-a-supplementary-data), but also possibly avoid any academic misconduct throughout the writing process.

### _6.3._ _The negative impacts of usage on SDL in academic English writing_

The quantitative results indicate that increased use of AI tools leads to decreased engagement in SDL among L2 learners in the 

academic writing process. This finding is different from what [Rashid and Asghar (2016)](#appendix-a-supplementary-data) have found in the general education context. Academic writing in English is a complex and demanding process, particularly for L2 learners who have to complete tasks within a limited time frame. If they rely heavily on AI for feedback and make corrections based on its suggestions or feedback, they may neglect using self-directed writing strategies. This explanation is supported by qualitative findings in the present study, which indicate that participants often critically evaluate AI-generated feedback to ensure responsible use and maintain academic integrity in their English writing. That is, instead of actively analyzing errors and making corrections, L2 learners might rely on AI suggestions, leading to less self-reflection and self-monitoring. The other possible explanation is that SDL is closely associated with writing motivation ([Wang et al., 2024)](#appendix-a-supplementary-data). Over-reliance on AI might diminish L2 learners’ sense of ownership over their academic writing, leading to decreased motivation and then less SDL in the writing process. In other words, excessive AI use in academic English writing may reduce the need for self-direction. A final note is about the non-significant relationship between evaluation and SDL. The ability to critically evaluate AI-generated information is a cognitive skill that involves assessing content quality, accuracy, or relevance. However, self-management and self-monitoring are metacognitive skills that involve setting goals, monitoring progress, and regulating the writing behavior (Zimmerman & Schunk, 2011). These two skills are theoretically distinct, and proficiency in one does not necessarily translate into the proficiency in the other. In general, AI literacy is related to SDL in academic English writing contexts, which echoes the theory of TPB ([Fishbein & Ajzen, 2011)](#appendix-a-supplementary-data).

### _6.4._ _Pedagogical implications_

Based on the findings of the current study, the following implications are provided. First, given the positive impacts of awareness of AI and ethical considerations on SDL as found in the current study, L2 writing instructors may consider integrating AI literacy edu- cation into academic writing curricula. Particularly, they can introduce certain fundamental concepts of AI in academic writing, ensuring that students understand how AI operates in this special context. As the present study found that AI usage negatively pre- dicted SDL, the appropriate use of AI tools in academic writing is significant. Instructors can show students how to critically use AI in each stage of writing—idea generation, planning, drafting, revising, and editing—without relying too heavily on it. For example, instructors may show how to use AI to brainstorm writing topics, but emphasize that students should refine and develop more insightful ideas on the basis of the generated topics. They may also analyze real-world cases of academic misconduct resulting from the misuse of AI tools and facilitate classroom discussions on ethical approaches to AI-assisted academic English writing. It is also necessary for L2 writing instructors to emphasize that students should have a balanced use of AI tools and treat them as supportive aids rather than as a replacement of their own cognition and metacognition. The cultivation of awareness and ethical consideration of AI, together with reduced reliance on AI, will encourage students to engage more in SDL activities, thereby reinforcing their development as self-directed and autonomous L2 writers. Additionally, instructors can focus on improving SDL directly by encouraging students to use specific AI functions for writing tasks (e.g., grammar checking), while taking responsibility for organizing, analyzing, editing, and refining their own work. Finally, as found in the present study, although AI was effective in providing timely written feedback, it had negative impacts on creativity. Therefore, L2 writing instructors should emphasize students’ critical engagement with feedback rather than passive acceptance. L2 learners must be guided to understand how to evaluate the accuracy and limitations of AI-generated content to ensure the development of higher-order thinking skills.

## 7. Conclusion and limitations

This study is the first to introduce the concept of AI literacy in the context of academic writing and to explore its influence on SDL. The findings indicate that AI awareness and ethical considerations positively impacted SDL, while AI usage negatively impacted it. The qualitative findings generally support the quantitative results and provide additional insights. This study contributes to the field by first introducing AI literacy into the context of academic writing and investigating its impacts on SDL. The mixed-methods findings provide new insights into the complex roles of AI in shaping learner autonomy, contributing to both theory and practice in AI-assisted writing instruction. Inevitably, this study has limitations. First, the sample size could be expanded to include a more diverse and representative group from multiple institutions. Second, this study has a gender imbalance among participants, as the majority were female in both the questionnaire survey and interview, which may affect the generalizability of the findings. Further studies could recruit a more gender-balanced sample to enhance generalizability. Third, the questionnaire data are cross-sectional, and future research could gather longitudinal data to establish a causal relationship between AI literacy and SDL in the context of academic English writing. Future studies can include additional variables as mediators in the SEM model of the present study to showcase a more comprehensive picture that depicts how AI literacy impacts SDL via these mediators. Despite these limitations, it is anticipated that this study contributes to the pedagogical advancement of academic English writing and informs the improvement of AI literacy and SDL in academic English writing.
